claims.text: The target alloy is an equimolar W–Mo–Ta–Nb–V refractory high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy composition is W30Mo30Ta30Nb10V10.
Arc melting followed by homogenization at 1200 °C produces an average grain size of approximately 50 µm.
Mechanical alloying and hot isostatic pressing after adding 0.5 wt% Y2O3 will produce a uniform dispersion of approximately 10 nm oxide particles.
The approximately 10 nm Y2O3 dispersoids will remain stable at grain boundaries and within grains.
Y2O3 particles will impede dislocation motion through Orowan strengthening.
Oxide sites will trap helium and self-interstitial defects under irradiation.
Defect trapping by the oxide sites will reduce irradiation-induced void nucleation and growth.
Adding 0.5 wt% Y2O3 will increase yield strength at 800 °C by approximately 30% relative to the oxide-free alloy.
Adding 0.5 wt% Y2O3 will reduce irradiation-induced swelling by approximately 50% after irradiation to 1 dpa at 800 °C.
The Y2O3 addition will not compromise thermal stability at 800 °C.
The intervention will be effective from 700 to 900 °C and at irradiation doses up to 5 dpa.
Above 900 °C, dispersoid coarsening may diminish the strengthening effect.
The stability of oxide dispersoids under sustained high-flux irradiation in refractory high-entropy alloys has not been fully established.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the W–Mo–Ta–Nb–V alloy equimolar, but the initial-state formula gives unequal W30Mo30Ta30Nb10V10 proportions. Moreover, those nominal subscripts sum to 110 rather than 100, so they are not directly valid atomic percentages without normalization.
